value.overview: The Solitary Sandpiper is a small, slender shorebird usually seen alone along freshwater edges. It breeds in northern North America and migrates through much of the United States, Mexico, Central America, and northern South America. Unlike most sandpipers, it commonly nests in abandoned songbird nests in trees rather than on the ground. Its distinctive white eye-ring, dark wings, white underparts, and habit of bobbing its rear body help identify it.
value.classification: The Solitary Sandpiper belongs to the sandpiper family Scolopacidae and the genus Tringa. Two commonly recognized subspecies are Tringa solitaria solitaria and Tringa solitaria cinnamomea.
value.identification: This robin-sized sandpiper measures about 20–23 cm long. Adults have olive-brown to gray-brown upperparts, white underparts, a bold complete white eye-ring, and relatively dark legs. Fine pale spotting is often visible on the back, especially in breeding plumage. In flight, the underwings appear dark and the rump and tail show dark-and-white barring. It differs from the similar Spotted Sandpiper by lacking a white wing stripe and by having a complete eye-ring.
value.rangeHabitat: The Solitary Sandpiper breeds across boreal Canada and Alaska and migrates south through the United States, Mexico, and Central America to wintering areas in northern and central South America. In Costa Rica it is a nonbreeding migrant and winter visitor, generally uncommon and more often found inland than on beaches. Suitable sites include quiet ponds, marshes, wooded swamps, streams, drainage ditches, flooded fields, and small temporary pools with muddy margins and nearby vegetation.
value.migrationStatus: Costa Rica lies within the species’ migration and wintering range. Individuals may occur there during both southbound and northbound migration, with some remaining through the northern winter; it does not normally breed in Costa Rica.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place in northern forests, bogs, muskeg, and wet woodland near ponds or small streams. The species usually lays three to five eggs in an old nest made by another bird, often in a tree or shrub. The female may modify the selected nest, and incubation lasts roughly 23–24 days. Chicks hatch covered in down, leave the nest soon after hatching, and are not known to receive food directly from their parents.
value.dietFeeding: The Solitary Sandpiper feeds mainly in shallow water and along muddy edges. Its prey includes aquatic and terrestrial insects, insect larvae, beetles, grasshoppers, dragonfly nymphs, spiders, worms, small crustaceans, snails, other mollusks, and occasionally tadpoles or small frogs. It picks prey from the surface, probes soft mud, and may tremble a foot or stir the substrate to expose small animals.
value.behavior: This species is characteristically solitary, although several birds may use the same wetland. It walks deliberately through shallow water, periodically bobbing its rear body and sometimes trembling its tail or feet while foraging. When disturbed, it may rise almost vertically and fly a short distance before settling again. It often uses quiet wetlands with limited shorebird activity and may also occur at small, temporary pools far from large bodies of water.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not precisely known because the species is dispersed and difficult to monitor, but it is not currently considered threatened.
